items.content:
Drunken Korean bar rant: 

Perhaps the most important takeaway from @unpromptedsf is the widening disconnect between demonstrated AI capability & the narrative being constructed around it.

Frontier AI labs & their financial backers have a vested interest in weaponizing the credibility of exceptional researchers, turning legitimate breakthroughs into the perception that AI possesses capabilities it has yet to reliably demonstrate. Fear, hype, & the promise of technological superiority are powerful instruments for shaping public perception, influencing markets, & attracting investment.

Yet much of this impressive research remains fundamentally dependent on years of human expertise, technical intuition, & highly specialized domain knowledge. These are not incidental contributions. They are often the very reason these breakthroughs are possible in the 1st place.

The work coming out of labs like @calif_io is a perfect textbook example. Their research deserves genuine recognition & respect. Many of the people behind it are figures I have admired for years, as have countless others in our industry. That admiration, however, should not exempt the commercial interests funding & promoting their work from scrutiny. Their motivations, incentives, and ultimate objectives deserve far more attention.

We should be able to celebrate meaningful advances in AI without allowing frontier labs to repackage exceptional human achievement as evidence of autonomous machine capability. Recognizing the value of AI should never require diminishing the expertise of the researchers making these advances possible.

There is a fundamental difference between advancing science and manufacturing the perception of progress. Increasingly, the latter appears to be the more lucrative business.

What concerns me most is how effectively this narrative has drawn some of our industry's most respected figures into its orbit, lending their hard-earned credibility to a marketing machine whose interests may not necessarily align with their own.

And judging by the public reaction, it's working remarkably well... Sadly

RT @Huntio: PHP2Shell One Week Later: Honeypot Shells on the Web, a Path to Root on Palo Alto Firewalls 

One week after the #php2shell patch, around 25 internet-facing #PaloAlto firewalls have been rooted, the first confirmed production compromises. On the open internet, the same bug is still only landing shells on honeypots.

We pivoted from the public exploitation reports into our AttackCapture open-directory data to see who is running it. 

What we found:

- ~25 internet-facing Palo Alto PAN-OS firewalls rooted, the first confirmed production compromises. Reported by Dream Research, verified by Unit 42, matched in operator logs we captured.
- The chain is two bugs: php2shell lands as nobody on the PAN-OS management interface, then a kernel bug (Fragnesia, CVE-2026-46300) escalates to root.
- On the open web, watchTowr, 0x4D31, and GreyNoise see shells only on honeypots. Wiz and CrowdStrike found none.
- 616 php2shell files across live open directories: a shared ASLR-bypass kit byte-identical across four hosts, a custom heap exploit with a log cleaner, and cloned PoCs.
- One operator handed the exploit research to an AI assistant and left the session log exposed.

Full research, IOCs, and detection guidance 👇

items.content:
Cursor users: check your Claude Code extension.

Cursor confirms a trojanized Anthropic.claude-code v2.1.313 in its extension marketplace on 29 October, 09:27 to 20:35 UTC. It estimates up to 5,000 affected users and identifies macOS ARM64 and Windows x64 builds.

Loading the extension executes malicious code that collects host information and attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor.

Cursor says SSH access would fail on most hosts due to bugs and insufficient privileges. That limits remote access; it doesn’t undo malicious code execution. Credentials and repositories accessible to that account are potentially at risk.

The package has been removed and the C2 taken offline. Uninstalling the extension may still leave persistence behind.

If this version ran, investigate the host, remove persistence and rotate accessible credentials from a clean system. Updating the extension alone doesn’t prove the machine is clean.

The vendor-confirmed distribution channel is Cursor’s marketplace. Microsoft VS Code uses a separate store. These reports don’t establish a compromised Microsoft Marketplace or malicious npm release.

My recommendation: turn off automatic extension updates completely - for yourself and for your developers. With supply chain attacks like this, I don’t think the benefit of another feature or a minor UI fix justifies automatically accepting every new release onto developer machines.

Update manually when something stops working, when a bug is actually getting in your way, or when a relevant security fix needs to be applied. Otherwise, leave a working extension alone.

items.content:
The employee cleared the browser history before handing the Windows laptop to the investigation team.

At first glance, there was nothing useful left. No suspicious download entry. No obvious website in the browser.

Then we checked the Windows DNS client cache.

Windows temporarily stores recently resolved domain names so it does not have to query a DNS server repeatedly. In the image, the cache still contains https://t.co/aPxZiAauT3, its A record, the resolved IP address and the remaining time-to-live.

This does not prove that the employee visited the domain in a browser. Another application, background service or security tool could have requested the same DNS resolution. The cache also does not identify exactly when the lookup occurred.

But it gives an investigator a valuable lead that can be correlated with firewall logs, proxy records, process telemetry and DNS server logs.

Browser history belongs to the browser. DNS evidence can exist elsewhere in the operating system.

Useful PowerShell command:

Get-DnsClientCache

items.content:
OpenAI is reportedly offering huge money to buy out smaller HFT firms and companies like [redacted], because they realize that they really do need more data that is handcrafted, high quality, high performance code in order to improve coding performance of the models. 

GitHub slop, vibeslop synthetic self-licking-ice cream-cone data and even what many AI-bros wrongly thought of as high quality open source code (like the Linux kernel ~lol~) is not improving the quality of the code that their models are producing. 

The reward-hacking behavior towards “just make the code compile to earn your reward” has been proven to be extremely counter-productive. 

Current SOTA models struggle to maintain coherent awareness of critical performance concepts like cache locality, branch prediction, instruction-level parallelism, memory ordering, false sharing, lock contention, vectorization, NUMA topology and the actual cost of moving data through a modern memory hierarchy. 

People will tell you that this stuff doesn’t matter, because modern compilers are so good. And in a normal world, I would concur with this sentiment. Normally, it would be true. In today’s world, you don’t need to really panic about a few too many if statements, because compilers will optimize away the cost. But these models, some how, some way, have an uncanny ability to write code that is SO bad, that not even the compilers can fix it. 

Their understanding of I/O performance is arguably even worse. They routinely generate code that is almost completely oblivious to storage hardware: pathological write amplification, excessive fsync() calls, unnecessary serialization, unbounded logging, tiny synchronous writes, redundant disk operations and utterly incompetent batching and buffering strategies.

Under sustained high-performance workloads, these pathologies can go well beyond merely degrading throughput. They can generate enough unnecessary physical I/O to accelerate SSD wear, exhaust write endurance, and contribute to premature drive failure. I’ve recently experienced hardware failure myself when I stupidly trusted GPT-6 to write and run a high throughput data service.

Which leads one to wonder… with trillions of tokens’ worth of newly vibecoded, I/O-oblivious software now finding its way into production environments, including the major hyperscale clouds, has anyone actually examined whether this phenomenon is beginning to materially affect storage-device failure rates?

And this is to say nothing of their performance at higher levels of abstraction. 

The conventional wisdom is that these models are much better at Python, JavaScript and the various higher-level frameworks than they are at systems programming. People who spend most of their time in that world will even confidently proclaim that “coding is solved.”

But consider the extraordinary irony that OpenAI’s own ChatGPT/Codex desktop applications, built around JavaScript frameworks, have been the subject of repeated, frequent, catastrophic resource-management failures.

Most commonly, runaway memory consumption reaching tens of gigabytes, psychotic background I/O loops, and SQLite logging behavior that has generated tens or even hundreds of gigabytes of disk writes during ordinary application use. Megaspeed CEO Huang Xiaole (黄小乐) aka Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, was found to be a Chinese intelligence asset funneling information to Beijing. President Trump was briefed and took no action.

American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence. Surveillance of Alice Huang revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive.

The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Jensen Huang set off alarms at the White House.

Roughly a year ago, Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China.

American officials already suspected that Alice Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced AI chips.

But the revelation that she was feeding information directly to Beijing raised more troubling possibilities. And it left questions about whether she could be gleaning information about Nvidia, which as much as any company accounts for the lead the US has maintained in developing cutting-edge AI models.

Jensen Huang has not received a defensive briefing, warnings sometimes given to Americans who are being targeted by foreign intelligence services.

The surveillance of Alice Huang continues, and companies that have been affiliated with her continued this year to purchase Nvidia chips.

When Trump was initially briefed on the intelligence last year, U.S. officials did not believe the Nvidia executive knew that Jensen Huang was gathering information for the Chinese. It is unclear whether intelligence officials have since updated their assessment, but some senior officials inside the Trump administration doubt that Jensen Huang could have remained unaware of what they had concluded was her intel-gathering role for China.

The previous reporting about Alice Huang described her meteoric and somewhat mysterious rise. A Chinese businesswoman and investor, she eventually became a top official with Megaspeed, which the Commerce Department, toward the end of the Biden administration, began to suspect was helping China evade US prohibitions and gain access to the computing power of Nvidia chips.

The US government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data center in Malaysia and found the site to be suspicious. The Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes, suggesting it was being shipped in or out rather than installed there.

Singapore has conducted its own investigation into Megaspeed. In 2025, Singaporean authorities brought Alice Huang in for questioning, but subsequently released her.

The Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed was handed over this year to the Justice Department.

Megaspeed is among the firms in Southeast Asia that buy chips to build data centers and then rent their computing power to companies in China.

Megaspeed is essentially a middle man. It has bought Nvidia chips from Aivres, the US arm of 🇨🇳 Inspur, which has been blacklisted for funneling technology to the Chinese military, though Aivres remains free of sanctions.

Megaspeed has then provided that computing power to Alibaba and other Chinese companies. US officials believe the firm is one piece of a sprawling international effort by Chinese companies to access the chips needed to build and run AI. Investigators suspect that some Nvidia chips acquired by Megaspeed are also finding their way illegally into China.

Two posts today. The one about an 11-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability got far more attention than the one about CAIRN/ARTEX.

I think the second topic is far more important.

I’ve been following vulnerabilities long enough to recognize the pattern. They’re discovered, exploited, patched, and replaced by the next ones. AI will accelerate this process dramatically, but the fundamental cycle remains the same.

What we’re seeing with AI-driven attack frameworks is something different. They’re starting to change how attacks are conducted in general, not just how vulnerabilities are discovered or exploited.

They allow attackers to plan, adapt, make decisions, and scale entire operations with far less human effort. And vulnerability exploitation is just a small part of what these systems can do.

I think this will have a much more profound and lasting impact on cybersecurity than the current wave of AI-discovered vulnerabilities.

Yet the individual CVE gets all the attention.
